name: ΔMARS Lab
headline: Robots That Cooperate, Manipulate, and Interact.
intro: At ΔMARS Lab, we investigate how robots collaborate and interact with the physical world. From autonomous cable manipulation and robotic knotting to cooperative aerial transportation and blimp systems, our research combines modeling, perception, planning, and control to develop new capabilities for autonomous robots.
overview:
ΔMARS Lab studies cooperative robotics, physical interaction, and autonomous manipulation. We investigate how individual robots and teams coordinate their actions, manipulate objects, and establish useful physical relationships with their environments. Our research connects dynamics, control, perception, and planning across aerial and ground platforms, including multirotor vehicles, autonomous blimps, and heterogeneous robotic teams.

Cable-based manipulation and robotic knotting form a distinctive focus within this broader agenda. Cables, ropes, and knots are not only objects to manipulate: they can become mechanisms for establishing connections, distributing forces, securing payloads, and creating mechanical constraints. We investigate autonomous cable routing, hitch and knot formation, interlacing, tension regulation, and friction-based grasping alongside broader questions of contact-rich interaction and cooperative autonomy.

Our approach combines mathematical foundations, algorithms, and experimental systems. Models guide planning and feedback, while physical experiments reveal where assumptions need refinement. This cycle connects scientific understanding with robotic behavior and supports research beyond any single mechanism or platform. Directed by Dr. Diego S. D’Antonio, the laboratory is part of Oakland University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering in Rochester, Michigan.
mission: Advance cooperative robotics and autonomous manipulation through modeling, perception, planning, control, and experiments, with a distinctive focus on cables, knots, and contact-rich interactions.
vision: Enable robots to cooperate and exploit physical interactions—including cables, ropes, and knots—to accomplish complex manipulation and transportation tasks across aerial and ground platforms.
principles: We build explicit models of geometry, dynamics, contact, and uncertainty. Assumptions and operating conditions remain visible so that analysis supports interpretable design decisions.
Perception, planning, and control work together. Measurements inform task decisions, and planned actions account for the forces and constraints that controllers must manage.
We use robot experiments to examine where models hold and where they fail. Measured behavior, reproducible procedures, and honest reporting guide the next iteration.
culture: We value questions that can be tested, models that can be challenged, and experiments that others can understand. Students contribute through analysis, software, hardware, and scientific writing. Collaboration across disciplines and careful mentorship support learning; clear attribution, reproducible procedures, and honest reporting remain part of everyday research.
bio: Dr. Diego S. D’Antonio is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Oakland University, where he directs the ΔMARS Lab. He received his Ph.D. in Computer Science and Engineering from Lehigh University. His research focuses on autonomous and cooperative robotics, physical interaction, and robotic manipulation, with particular emphasis on aerial robotics, multi-robot systems, and cable-based manipulation. His work explores the integration of knot theory, contact mechanics, dynamics, planning, and control to enable autonomous grasping, object attachment, and cooperative transportation. His broader interests include contact-rich robotic interaction, autonomous blimps, and robotic systems for space applications. His research has received support from the Michigan Space Grant Consortium, and he is actively involved in student mentoring, robotics education, and STEM outreach.

research.title: Cooperative Robotics
research.short: We study coordination, cooperative control, and collaborative manipulation using teams of autonomous robots across aerial, ground, and heterogeneous platforms.
research.detail: Cooperative robotics asks how a team can achieve tasks beyond the capabilities of its individual members. We investigate coordination, cooperative control, collaborative manipulation, and the distribution of motion and physical forces. Shared objects and flexible connections can mechanically couple robots, while heterogeneous platforms introduce different capabilities and constraints. Research includes cooperative transportation, formation control, and distributed decision-making across aerial and ground systems. The challenge is to connect collective task objectives with feasible actions at each robot. This theme draws on models of interaction, perception, and planning, with cable-mediated cooperation as one distinctive area of investigation.
questions: How can a robot team distribute forces while maintaining a desired object motion?
What information must robots exchange to coordinate through shared cables?
How should cooperation adapt when a contact changes or one robot reaches an actuation limit?
applications: Distributed handling of large or flexible structures
research.visual: Show synchronized trajectories and force arrows over a real transportation experiment; label each robot’s role.

research.title: Cable Manipulation and Robotic Knotting
research.short: We investigate autonomous cable routing, hitch and knot formation, interlacing, and manipulation of flexible linear objects for grasping and securement.
research.detail: Cables, ropes, and knots can act as mechanisms that enable robotic tasks. We investigate how robots route flexible linear objects, form hitches and knots, regulate tension, and exploit friction to establish attachments and secure payloads. The challenge is to connect the geometry of a cable arrangement with its mechanical behavior: a route must be achievable, and the resulting contact must support the intended task. Research includes cable interlacing, entanglement, grasp formation, and cooperative handling. This distinctive focus connects modeling, perception, planning, and control while contributing to the laboratory’s broader agenda in autonomous manipulation and physical interaction.
questions: How can robots plan and execute cable routes that form useful hitches or knots?
How do tension, friction, and contact geometry determine whether a cable attachment supports a task?
How can a robot team form, inspect, and release cable-based connections autonomously?
research.visual: Pair an actual cable-interlacing experiment with a labeled knot or hitch diagram showing routing, contact regions, and tension. Distinguish knot geometry from measured attachment behavior.

research.title: Physical Interaction
research.short: We study how robots model, sense, and control contact with objects and environments to perform physically constrained manipulation tasks.
research.detail: Physical interaction changes how a robot can move and what it can accomplish. We investigate contact between robots, objects, and environments, including attachment, pushing, grasping, and manipulation of rigid or flexible structures. Contact may establish a useful constraint, transmit a force, or introduce uncertainty through friction and slipping. Our research connects interaction sensing with models and feedback so robots can respond to changing conditions. The scientific challenge is to plan and regulate contact as part of the task, rather than consider motion alone. This theme spans aerial and ground platforms and connects cooperative action with autonomous manipulation.
questions: How can robots establish and regulate useful contact while maintaining stable behavior?
Which measurements reveal contact geometry, slipping, and interaction forces?
How should manipulation plans adapt when contact constraints change?
research.visual: Use an actual contact sequence and synchronized force or state measurements; add a schematic identifying the contact region and constraints.

research.title: Dynamics and Control
research.short: We develop models and feedback methods for robotic systems whose behavior changes with contact, friction, cable tension, and mechanical coupling.
research.detail: Robotic systems change their behavior when contacts are established, released, or rearranged. We develop models and control methods for nonlinear dynamics, hybrid systems, contact mechanics, friction, and mechanical coupling across aerial and ground platforms. Cables and suspended loads provide important examples: tension, slack, and changing geometry connect robot motion to object behavior. The challenge is to retain the physical variables that matter while keeping models useful for estimation, planning, and feedback. Stability analysis and experimental validation guide our approach. This theme supplies foundations for cooperative robotics, knotting and cable manipulation, and broader contact-rich autonomous tasks.
questions: Which interaction variables are necessary for a useful reduced-order model?
How can controllers account for transitions between slack, tension, sticking, and sliding?
What stability and feasibility conditions can guide manipulation under changing contacts?
research.visual: Use an annotated cable diagram linked to a tension-versus-time trace; visually distinguish measured data from schematic examples.

research.title: Perception and Planning
research.short: We connect perception, estimation, and task planning so robots can decide when to observe, move, or manipulate their surroundings.
research.detail: Autonomous physical interaction requires robots to decide what to measure and how to act when the environment is only partly known. We investigate state estimation, sensor fusion, active perception, manipulation planning, and task-level decision-making. Actions may change both an object’s position and the information available about it: moving an obstacle can reveal a target, while adjusting a cable can expose an interaction state. The challenge is to close the loop between observations, physically feasible plans, and feedback control. This theme supports aerial and cooperative tasks while leaving room for exploratory work in robotic search and object retrieval.
questions: When should a robot observe again rather than execute its current plan?
How can pushing or rearranging objects reveal a hidden target?
How can planning use estimates of contact geometry and interaction uncertainty?
research.visual: Use a labeled observe–plan–act sequence with camera views and estimated states; mark illustrative scenes as concepts.

projects.title: Autonomous Aerial Grasping Through Cable Interlacing
projects.subtitle: Using cables to form a grasp
projects.status: Published research · IEEE Transactions on Robotics, 2026
projects.brief: This project investigates how multiple aerial robots arrange and interlace cables around an object to establish an attachment for lifting and transportation. It connects cable routing, contact and friction mechanics, and team coordination. Cable-based grasp formation offers a way to explore securement without relying on a conventional rigid gripper.
projects.extended:
A cable can connect aerial robots to an object while also acting as the mechanism that establishes a grasp. This project investigates how a team of UAVs can route and interlace cables around an object, form a hitch, and transition toward lifting and transportation. The task links geometry with mechanics: a feasible cable path does not by itself establish that an attachment will sustain the required load.

The research concept brings together coordinated robot motion, cable–cable and cable–object contact, friction, and grasp formation. A useful approach must account for how cable routing changes during the maneuver and how the resulting interaction constrains the robots. Modeling and planning therefore need to inform each other, with physical tests used to assess the assumptions behind securement.

The intended contribution is an integrated understanding of autonomous cable-based attachment and cooperative aerial handling. The associated paper, “From Hitch to Lift,” appears in IEEE Transactions on Robotics; its bibliographic record and cable-interlacing footage were supplied by the author. Specific performance claims are reserved for evidence from the full paper. Historical experiments will retain their original institutional attribution.
projects.challenge: Form an attachment that is both geometrically achievable and mechanically adequate while coordinating multiple flying robots.
projects.approach: Connect cable-routing plans, contact models, and coordinated control; compare the predicted attachment behavior with physical trials.
projects.contributions: Intended contributions: interaction-aware grasp formation and an integrated attachment-to-transport workflow. Demonstrated outcomes require source verification.

projects.video: An author-approved, continuous sequence of approach, hitch formation, lift, and release; identify the original experiment location.

projects.title: Cooperative Aerial Transportation with Sliding Cable Attachments
projects.subtitle: Coordinating a load as cable geometry changes
projects.brief: This project studies cooperative payload transportation when a cable can slide through an attachment on the load. Changing cable distribution couples robot motion, payload dynamics, and interaction forces. An author-posted preprint reports a dual-quadrotor system, geometry-based reference generation, and experimental demonstrations of the approach.
projects.extended:
A moving cable attachment introduces another variable into cooperative aerial transportation: the cable’s distribution between the robots changes as the system moves. This project studies how that changing geometry affects the relationship between vehicle motion and payload motion. The scientific question is how a team can maintain a useful transportation configuration while respecting cable constraints and available actuation.

The author-posted preprint describes a single cable passing through a payload-mounted hook and reports physical experiments. Its models and reference-generation approach provide a starting point for examining mechanically coupled transport. The broader research direction asks how planning and feedback can use the changing geometry rather than assume that every attachment remains fixed.

For the website, the experiment should be explained through synchronized views of robot motion, cable distribution, and payload behavior. A schematic can introduce the mechanism before a real video shows its operation. Performance values, equipment details, and claims about robustness should be added only with the authors’ selected evidence. The current entry is labeled as a preprint and does not imply conference acceptance or journal publication.
projects.challenge: Account for changing cable distribution while coordinating payload motion and satisfying physical constraints.
projects.approach: Use coupled geometry and dynamics to generate feasible robot references; examine their behavior in physical transport experiments.
projects.contributions: The preprint reports a dual-quadrotor sliding-hook system and experimental evaluation. No numerical performance or broader reliability claim is added.
projects.photo: Full-system view with both robots, the cable, and the payload-mounted hook visible.
projects.video: Continuous transport sequence with a synchronized schematic showing cable redistribution.
projects.animation: A labeled geometric diagram showing cable distribution as the vehicles move.

projects.title: Cooperative Blimp Swarms for Space-Debris Capture Emulation
projects.subtitle: Studying selected capture interactions in a terrestrial testbed
projects.status: Research direction · project stage to confirm
projects.brief: This project explores lightweight robotic blimps as platforms for studying selected aspects of cooperative capture and transportation. The research concept involves coordinated motion, interaction with moving objects, and cable-mediated handling. Blimp experiments can support controlled studies of these interactions; they do not reproduce true orbital microgravity dynamics.
projects.extended:
Cooperative capture involves more than approaching an object. Robots must coordinate their relative motion, establish a useful interaction, and manage the consequences of contact. This research direction explores robotic blimps as terrestrial platforms for examining selected aspects of those tasks, including interaction with moving or tumbling objects and cable-mediated transportation.

Lightweight aerial platforms offer a setting in which sensing, coordination, and attachment strategies can be investigated together. A study could compare planned relative motion with observed contact behavior, examine how a team distributes roles, and test how capture geometry changes during a maneuver. These are proposed experimental questions; the website should report the testbed configuration and completed milestones only after confirmation.

The emulation scope must remain explicit. Buoyancy, aerodynamic drag, gravity, and actuation constraints shape blimp motion differently from orbital systems. The value of the platform lies in examining selected cooperative behaviors and interactions, with those differences stated alongside each demonstration. Michigan Space Grant Consortium support is identified in the supplied brief, but the project-specific award, period, acknowledgment, and current research stage remain to be confirmed.
projects.challenge: Coordinate contact with a moving object while defining which aspects of capture the terrestrial platform can meaningfully emulate.
projects.approach: Proposed approach: develop relative-motion models, cooperative control, and cable-based interactions; evaluate selected behaviors in a documented terrestrial testbed.
projects.contributions: Expected contributions: cooperative capture strategies and an experimental framework with explicit emulation limits. No completed capture result is claimed.
projects.photo: Real blimps and target object in the test area; include scale and facility context once available.
projects.video: A selected capture maneuver with labels identifying robot roles and emulation limits.
projects.animation: Relative-motion and cable-interaction diagrams; avoid orbital footage presented as a blimp result.
projects.funding: Michigan Space Grant Consortium support supplied by the user; project-specific award and acknowledgment pending confirmation.

projects.title: Cable Interaction Sensing and Control
projects.subtitle: Observing the physical interaction state
projects.status: Research direction · project stage to confirm
projects.brief: Robot motion alone may not reveal whether a cable is taut, slipping, or contacting an object. This research direction develops sensing and modeling strategies for cable interaction, including tension, angle, and contact geometry. The goal is to connect reduced-order interaction estimates with feedback control and manipulation decisions.
projects.extended:
A robot’s position does not necessarily reveal the condition of the cable it is manipulating. Similar vehicle configurations may correspond to different tensions, contact locations, or frictional states. This research direction asks which measurements and reduced-order variables can make those differences observable and useful for feedback.

Topics include tension sensing, cable-angle measurement, contact geometry estimation, and transitions between interaction modes. A proposed workflow links sensor measurements to a compact description of the robot–cable–object system, then uses that description to inform control and planning. The scientific challenge is to preserve the variables that affect task behavior while avoiding a model that is too complex to estimate reliably.

Experimental storytelling should connect an observable event to its measurement: a cable becomes taut, a contact begins to slide, or an attachment changes geometry. A synchronized video and sensor trace can explain why robot motion alone is insufficient. Specific sensors, estimation accuracy, control methods, and hardware implementations are not yet confirmed. The website therefore presents this work as a research direction and reserves result statements for documented experiments.
projects.challenge: Identify interaction variables that are observable from practical measurements and sufficient to support useful feedback.
projects.approach: Proposed approach: combine sensing, reduced-order models, and contact-state estimation, then examine closed-loop behavior in experiments.
projects.contributions: Expected contributions: interpretable interaction estimates and sensor-informed control. No sensing accuracy or validated hardware capability is claimed.
projects.photo: Close-up of an actual cable interface and sensor installation once confirmed.
projects.video: An experiment synchronized with measured tension and estimated contact states.
projects.animation: A clearly labeled schematic of slack, tension, and sliding transitions.

projects.title: Autonomous Robotic Search and Manipulation
projects.subtitle: Using physical actions to reveal and retrieve objects
projects.brief: This exploratory direction combines active perception, scene understanding, and physical manipulation to search for and retrieve objects. A robot may need to move an obstacle before it can observe or grasp a target. We investigate how observations and actions can inform each other in a closed-loop autonomous process.
projects.extended:
Object search becomes a manipulation problem when the target cannot be seen or reached directly. This exploratory direction considers robots that use observations to select actions and use actions to acquire new information. Pushing an obstacle may reveal a hidden object; changing a viewpoint may expose a grasp opportunity without altering the scene.

The research concept connects active visual perception, mapping, mechanical search, grasp planning, and closed-loop decision-making. A central challenge is choosing between gathering information and committing to physical action. Plans must account for what the robot knows, what an action may reveal, and whether the resulting contact or grasp is physically feasible.

This direction extends the laboratory’s focus on physical interaction beyond a particular aerial platform. It offers a way to connect perception and planning with the consequences of manipulation. No completed search system, benchmark result, or platform is asserted. Initial website media should use labeled conceptual diagrams until real experiments are available; subsequent project updates can document the chosen task, operating conditions, observed outcomes, and remaining limitations.
projects.challenge: Decide when to observe, rearrange the scene, or attempt retrieval under incomplete information.
projects.approach: Proposed approach: combine active perception, scene-state estimation, action selection, and grasp planning in a closed loop.
projects.contributions: Expected contributions: information-aware search and manipulation strategies. This is exploratory work with no completed accomplishment claimed.
projects.photo: Actual workspace before and after an occluding object is moved, once experiments exist.
projects.video: Observe–push–observe–grasp sequence, with pauses explaining each decision.
projects.animation: A concept diagram showing how pushing changes visibility and available grasps.

positioning: Cooperative Robotics, Physical Interaction, and Autonomous Manipulation
supporting_line: Advancing autonomous robotics through cooperative coordination, physical interaction, and intelligent manipulation.
question: How can autonomous multi-robot systems coordinate their actions and leverage contact dynamics and mechanical interactions with deformable linear objects—including cable tension, friction, and topological constraints—to enable complex manipulation capabilities beyond those achievable by individual robots?

featured_focus.title: Cable Manipulation and Robotic Knotting
featured_focus.subtitle: Enabling robots to manipulate flexible structures and exploit their mechanical properties.
paragraphs: We investigate how autonomous robots can manipulate cables, ropes, and other deformable linear objects to establish physical connections, secure objects, and perform complex manipulation tasks.
Our research explores autonomous hitch and knot formation, cable interlacing, tension regulation, contact mechanics, and friction-based grasping.

By combining mathematical modeling, planning, control, and experimental robotics, we seek to enable robots to exploit the mechanical properties of flexible materials for manipulation and cooperative transportation.
